model_raw_board_events.text: Substituent Effects on Carboxylic Acid Strength
Acidity depends on conjugate base (carboxylate) stability. Substituents near the carboxyl group can either stabilise or destabilise the carboxylate by the inductive effect.
Electron-withdrawing groups (EWGs) pull electron density away through sigma bonds (-I effect). This spreads the negative charge on the carboxylate, stabilising it and increasing acidity.
Electron-donating groups (EDGs) push electron density toward the carboxylate (+I effect). This concentrates negative charge, destabilising the anion and decreasing acidity.

model_raw_board_events.text: Common Pitfalls and Exam Strategies
Pitfall 1: Reasoning from the neutral acid instead of the conjugate base. Acidity is decided by how well the anion holds the negative charge — always argue from carboxylate stability.
Pitfall 2: Ignoring inductive distance. A halogen on the alpha carbon strengthens the acid far more than the same halogen on beta or gamma; induction decays steeply along the chain.
Pitfall 3: Thinking NaBH4 reduces -COOH. It does not — NaBH4 is too weak. Use LiAlH4 or diborane; diborane spares esters, nitro and halo groups, LiAlH4 does not.

model_raw_board_events.text: Why Alpha-Hydrogens Are Special
A carbonyl compound has two reactive sites: the carbonyl carbon (electron-poor, electrophilic) and the alpha-carbon (its hydrogens are unusually acidic).
Shop analogy: the carbonyl carbon is the front counter that attracts nucleophiles; the alpha-carbon is the back counter where the acidic hydrogens sit.
The alpha-hydrogens are acidic because a base can remove one, and the resulting negative charge is delocalised onto the electronegative oxygen by resonance.

Cannizzaro reaction: a disproportionation (self oxidation-reduction) of aldehydes that have NO alpha-hydrogen, carried out in concentrated alkali.
Disproportionation means one molecule is oxidised while another identical molecule is reduced in the same reaction.

When two different aldehydes without alpha-H are treated with concentrated alkali, one is oxidized to a carboxylate salt and the other is reduced to an alcohol. This is the crossed (or cross) Cannizzaro reaction.
The aldehyde that is attacked fastest by hydroxide becomes the hydride donor and is therefore oxidized. The other aldehyde accepts the hydride and is reduced.
Formaldehyde (HCHO) has the least hindered and most electrophilic carbonyl carbon among simple aldehydes, so hydroxide adds to it preferentially.

The SO2 adds to the dye and destroys the extended conjugation, so the magenta colour is lost.
An aldehyde binds the SO2, restoring the conjugation of the dye and bringing back the magenta colour.

model_raw_board_events.text: The Identification Chain: A Four-Station Decision Tree
Think like a diagnostic lab: run tests in a fixed order, each result narrows the field. Never rely on a single test.

Station 2 - Tollens' reagent: silver mirror = ALDEHYDE. No mirror = KETONE.

model_raw_board_events.text: The Two Reactive Sites of a Carbonyl
A carbonyl compound is not a one-trick molecule: it has two distinct reactive sites, and almost every named reaction is one of these two engines firing.
FRONT COUNTER = the carbonyl carbon. It is electron-poor (delta+) and electrophilic, so it attracts nucleophiles (electron-rich reagents).
BACK COUNTER = the alpha-carbon (the carbon next door). Its alpha-hydrogens are unusually acidic and can be removed by a base.

model_raw_board_events.text: Nucleophilic Addition: The Master Mechanism
The carbonyl carbon is delta-plus (electrophilic) and the oxygen is delta-minus, so electron-rich nucleophiles attack the carbon.
Step 1 - Attack: the nucleophile donates a lone pair into the pi-star of C=O, approaching perpendicular to the sp2 plane.
Step 2 - Rehybridisation: carbon goes sp2 to sp3, the pi electrons collapse onto oxygen, giving a tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate.

model_raw_board_events.text: Reduction and Oxidation: Choosing the Right Reagent
Toolbox idea: the carbonyl is the workpiece, the reagent is the tool. Pick the tool that does the job without damaging the rest of the molecule.
Reduction to alcohol: NaBH4 is mild (alcohol/water medium) and reduces aldehydes and ketones only, sparing esters, acids and nitro groups.
LiAlH4 is a strong hydride: it reduces aldehydes, ketones, esters, acids, nitriles and amides. Use it only when nothing else must survive.

model_raw_board_events.text: Reactivity Order Toward Nucleophilic Addition
Two factors decide how fast a nucleophile attacks the carbonyl carbon: steric hindrance (crowding) and electronic effects (size of the delta+ on carbon).

Electronic factor: alkyl groups are +I pushers that soften the delta+; a ketone has two such pushers, an aldehyde only one, so the aldehyde carbon stays more electrophilic.

model_raw_board_events.text: Nucleophilic Addition: The Master Mechanism
The carbonyl carbon is delta-plus (electrophilic), so a nucleophile attacks it. The pi bond of C=O is the electron pair that gets used up.
Step 1 - Attack: Nu-minus approaches the carbonyl carbon roughly perpendicular to the plane of the sp2 carbon and donates a lone pair into the pi-star orbital of C=O.

model_raw_board_events.text: The Boiling-Point Ladder: Why Carbonyls Sit Where They Do
Boiling means molecules letting go of each other and escaping as free gas-phase individuals. The stronger the intermolecular grip, the more energy needed, so the higher the boiling point.
The force ladder, weakest to strongest: van der Waals dispersion < dipole-dipole < hydrogen bond < double hydrogen-bonded dimer.

Aldehydes and ketones share the same dominant force: dipole-dipole attraction from the polar C=O, with no O-H donor. So their boiling points are close and must be settled by finer factors.
The classic isomeric pair: propanal (CH3CH2CHO) and acetone/propanone (CH3COCH3) are both C3H6O, molar mass 58.

Carboxylic acids sit at the TOP of the boiling-point ladder: hydrocarbon < ether < aldehyde/ketone < alcohol < carboxylic acid.

model_raw_board_events.text: Water Solubility: Head vs Tail
Every carbonyl molecule has two competing parts: a polar head that hydrogen-bonds with water, and a non-polar hydrocarbon tail that water rejects.
Polar head: the C=O oxygen accepts hydrogen bonds from water; a carboxylic acid's -OH can both donate and accept, making the head even stronger.
Hydrocarbon tail: a long alkyl or aryl portion is hydrophobic and pulls the molecule out of water.

The same force ladder that orders boiling points also tells you whether a carbonyl compound is a gas, liquid or solid at room temperature.
Weaker attractions and lower mass keep a compound gaseous or volatile; stronger attractions and greater mass pull it toward the solid end.

segment_objective: Explain why aromatic aldehydes, ketones, and acids are deactivating and meta-directing in electrophilic substitution.

model_raw_board_events.text: Aromatic Carbonyls: Deactivating and Meta-Directing
Aromatic aldehydes, ketones and acids still undergo electrophilic substitution at the ring, but the carbonyl-containing group changes both the rate and the position of attack.
The groups -CHO, -COR and -COOH are electron-withdrawing by induction (electronegative O pulls sigma electrons) and by resonance (the C=O pi system accepts electron density from the ring).

params.title: Why -CHO is meta-directing
steps: Step 1: -CHO withdraws e- by induction (O pulls sigma e-)
Step 2: -CHO withdraws e- by resonance (C=O accepts ring pi e-)
Step 3: Ring electron density falls -> ring deactivated
Step 4: Ortho/para attack puts + charge next to electron-poor C -> unstable
Step 5: Meta attack avoids this -> meta intermediate more stable
Conclusion: EWG on ring = deactivating + meta-directing

Functional group is -COOH (carboxyl = carbonyl + hydroxyl). The carboxyl carbon is sp2 with bond angles near 120 degrees.

model_raw_board_events.text: Esterification: Nucleophilic Acyl Substitution

Carboxylic acids do not undergo simple nucleophilic addition because resonance makes the carboxyl carbon less electrophilic. Instead, they undergo nucleophilic acyl substitution: the –OH group is replaced by –OR.
Step 1: Protonation of the carbonyl oxygen by the acid catalyst (H2SO4 or HCl) increases the electrophilicity of the carboxyl carbon.

model_raw_board_events.text: Aromatic Carboxylic Acids: Ring Deactivation and Meta-Direction
Benzoic acid is the reference aromatic carboxylic acid (pKa 4.19). The -COOH group is an electron-withdrawing group (EWG) on the ring.
The carboxyl carbon is sp2 and the C=O pi bond withdraws electron density from the ring by both induction (-I) and resonance (-M).
